{{< include _bayesammi-macros.txt >}}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# HTML figures are drawn as PNG and kept as WebP: lossless (the same pixels in about half the space of PNG), or
# lossy at quality 90 when that is less than half the size, as for traces and densities of thousands of draws. The
# PDF figures stay vector graphics. Any failure of magick (not installed, no WebP, or a broken installation whose
# system libraries are missing) keeps the PNG
webp <- function(path) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output() || !grepl(pattern = "[.]png$", x = path)) return(path)
  tryCatch(
      {
        if (!requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) || !isTRUE(magick::magick_config()$webp)) return(path)
        img <- magick::image_read(path)
        out <- sub(pattern = "[.]png$", replacement = ".webp", x = path)
        tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
        magick::image_write(
            image   = img
          , path    = out
          , format  = "webp"
          , quality = 100
          , defines = c(`webp:lossless` = "true")
          )
        magick::image_write(image = img, path = tmp, format = "webp", quality = 90)
        if (file.size(tmp) < file.size(out) / 2) file.copy(from = tmp, to = out, overwrite = TRUE)
        unlink(c(path, tmp))
        out
      }
    , error = function(e) path
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5,
                      dev = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "ragg_png", dpi = 96,
                      fig.process = webp)
if (requireNamespace("bayesammi", quietly = TRUE)) library(bayesammi) else
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

# Abstract

A least-squares AMMI biplot shows point estimates only. Its Bayesian counterpart gives every genotype and environment
a highest posterior density (HPD) region. A region that contains the origin marks a stable genotype or environment,
regions that overlap mark a homogeneous group, and the marginal interval on the first term decides the direction of
the interaction. This vignette shows how `biplots()` builds the regions and how to read them.

# The coordinates

For draw $s$ the point of genotype $i$ is
$\left(\lambda_1^{(s)1/2}\alpha^{(s)}_{i1}, \lambda_2^{(s)1/2}\alpha^{(s)}_{i2}\right)$. The draws
of a genotype form a cloud whose shape shows the uncertainty of its interaction.

```{r fit}
fit <-
  bayes_ammi(
      .data   = Maiz
    , .y      = y
    , .gen    = entry
    , .env    = site
    , .rep    = rep
    , .nIter  = 6000
    , .k      = 2
    , .burnin = 1000
    , .thin   = 1
    , .chains = 2
    , .priors = bam_priors(
          mu_mean     = 0
        , mu_var      = 1e+8
        , tau_mean    = 0
        , tau_var     = 1e+8
        , delta_mean  = 0
        , delta_var   = 1e+8
        , lambda_mean = 0
        , lambda_var  = 1e+8
        , nu          = 1
        , s2          = NULL
        )
    , .level  = 0.95
    , .seed   = 4
    , .align  = TRUE
    , .model  = "AMMI"
    , .het    = FALSE
    , .waic   = TRUE
    )
```

# HPD regions

A bivariate kernel density $\hat{f}$ is estimated from the cloud. The $100(1-p)\%$ HPD region is the set where
$\hat{f}$ exceeds the $p$-quantile of $\hat{f}$ at the draws, so it holds $100(1-p)\%$ of them and is the
smallest such set (Hyndman 1996). It contains the origin exactly when $\hat{f}(\mathbf{0})$ reaches that
quantile.

```{r regions, fig.width = 9}
bp <-
  biplots(
      model         = fit
    , burnin        = 0
    , thin          = 0.5
    , pb            = c(0.05, 0.01)
    , plot_stable   = TRUE
    , plot_unstable = TRUE
    , ncolors       = 5
    , .which        = "both"
    , .grid         = 100
    )
bp$biplot
```

# Stable genotypes and environments

```{r stable}
bp$biplot_data[, list(byplot, name, x, y, stable, axis1_lower, axis1_upper, group)]
```

* `stable = TRUE`: the 95% region contains the origin, so the interaction of the genotype (environment) is not
  different from zero on the two terms jointly.
* `group`: the marginal 95% HPD interval of the first coordinate. "positive" and "negative" groups interact in
  opposite directions; the paper uses this criterion.

A genotype can be stable in the joint sense and still have a first coordinate that differs from zero. This happens
when the second term is so uncertain that the region stretches over the origin along the second axis.

# Only the unstable ones

```{r unstable, fig.width = 9}
bp_u <-
  biplots(
      model         = fit
    , burnin        = 0
    , thin          = 0.5
    , pb            = 0.05
    , plot_stable   = FALSE
    , plot_unstable = TRUE
    , ncolors       = 5
    , .which        = "both"
    , .grid         = 100
    )
bp_u$biplot
```

# Reading genotype and environment together

A genotype yields more than its main effects predict in environments whose first scores have the same sign as its
own, and less where the signs differ. The genotypes in the positive group are therefore adapted to the environments
in the positive group.

```{r int}
bam_interpret(
    x             = bp
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , top           = 5
  )
```

# References

Crossa, J., Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D., Cotes, J. M., Viele, K., Liu, G. and Cornelius, P. L. (2011). Bayesian estimation of the additive main effects and multiplicative interaction model. *Crop Science*, 51(4), 1458--1469. doi:10.2135/cropsci2010.06.0343

Hyndman, R. J. (1996). Computing and graphing highest density regions. *The American Statistician*, 50(2), 120--126.
